case.label: C
case.text: The strongest rival is the persistent file system. A reader can argue that results are the valuable output and a persistent file system with daily backups protects them better than a scratch file system that holds data only until the job ends. But the stem says a failed server only means repeating a step from S3, the job lasts two weeks, and the question asks for the MOST cost-effective option, so paying for persistent storage and backups is not justified. B is a trap, not a rival, because a scratch file system does not take automatic backups, and A pays for provisioned throughput on EFS. Wording cues that give the answer away: 'short-lived', 'can read the input again and repeat the failed step', 'MOST cost-effective' and 'results must be written back to the bucket' all point to scratch plus export.

case.label: A
case.text: A reader can argue that copying the dataset into FSx for Lustre with DataSync gives the same very high throughput, and that a fully loaded file system has no first-read latency, so it is the safer design. But the stem says each job reads only part of the 200 TB and training must start as soon as possible, so waiting for a full copy fails the requirement and adds a DataSync task to run. A linked file system loads data on first access. The phrases 'reads only part of the dataset' and 'start as soon as possible' give D away. C and B do not give very high shared throughput.

case.label: B
case.text: FSx for NetApp ONTAP also serves NFS to Linux clients and offers snapshots and writable clones (FlexClone), so a reader could argue it is a second valid destination for a workload that needs fast writable copies. But the stem keeps the teams' existing ZFS snapshot-and-clone scripts unchanged, which fits FSx for OpenZFS directly, while ONTAP would need the scripts rewritten for NetApp tools. Also SnapMirror needs a NetApp source system, which an on-premises ZFS server is not, so the migration path in B does not work. The word 'ZFS' in the stem and the phrase 'writable copies from snapshots' give C away. A restores a full file system per copy, which is slow and heavy, and D is a copy, not a clone.
